examples.solution_text:
Divide by the main denominator by multiplying by its reciprocal.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{\frac{3}{x}}{\frac{9}{x^2}}\\&=\frac{3}{x}\times\frac{x^2}{9}\\&=\frac{3x^2}{9x}\\&=\frac{x}{3}\end{aligned}$
The original expression requires $x\ne0$.

The LCD of the small fractions is $x$. Multiply both main parts by $x$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{2+\frac{5}{x}}{3}\\&=\frac{x\left(2+\frac{5}{x}\right)}{3x}\\&=\frac{2x+5}{3x}\end{aligned}$
Here $x\ne0$.

Multiply both main parts by $x+4$, including the whole-number terms.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{7}{2-\frac{3}{x+4}}\\&=\frac{7(x+4)}{(x+4)\left(2-\frac{3}{x+4}\right)}\\&=\frac{7(x+4)}{2(x+4)-3}\\&=\frac{7(x+4)}{2x+5}\end{aligned}$
The original expression requires $x\ne-4,-\frac{5}{2}$.

The main numerator is $3-\frac{2}{x}$ and the main denominator is $2+\frac{5}{x}$. Multiply every term in both by $x$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{3-\frac{2}{x}}{2+\frac{5}{x}}\\&=\frac{x\left(3-\frac{2}{x}\right)}{x\left(2+\frac{5}{x}\right)}\\&=\frac{3x-2}{2x+5}\end{aligned}$
The original expression requires $x\ne0,-\frac{5}{2}$.

Use the LCD $x^2$, then factorise before cancelling.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{1-\frac{6}{x}}{1-\frac{36}{x^2}}\\&=\frac{x^2\left(1-\frac{6}{x}\right)}{x^2\left(1-\frac{36}{x^2}\right)}\\&=\frac{x^2-6x}{x^2-36}\\&=\frac{x(x-6)}{(x-6)(x+6)}\\&=\frac{x}{x+6}\end{aligned}$
Keep the original restrictions $x\ne0,6,-6$.

Multiply both main parts by the LCD $x(x+5)$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x+5}}{\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x+5}}\\&=\frac{x(x+5)\left(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x+5}\right)}{x(x+5)\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x+5}\right)}\\&=\frac{(x+5)+x}{(x+5)-x}\\&=\frac{2x+5}{5}\end{aligned}$
Here $x\ne0,-5$.

examples.question_text: Show that the average of $\frac{1}{n}$ and $\frac{1}{n+4}$ is $\frac{n+2}{n(n+4)}$.
examples.solution_text:
Add the two values and divide by $2$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n+4}}{2}\\&=\frac{n(n+4)\left(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n+4}\right)}{2n(n+4)}\\&=\frac{(n+4)+n}{2n(n+4)}\\&=\frac{2(n+2)}{2n(n+4)}\\&=\frac{n+2}{n(n+4)}\end{aligned}$
Here $n\ne0,-4$.

examples.derivation: Dividing gives (3/x)(x²/9)=x/3, with x≠0. This follows C3 Foundation Q1 and Q3's reciprocal method.
Multiplying both main parts by x gives (2x+5)/(3x), with x≠0. This adapts C3 Foundation Q2a–b.
Clearing x+4 gives 7(x+4)/[2(x+4)−3]=7(x+4)/(2x+5). Original denominators exclude x=−4 and x=−5/2. The supplied LCD rule and binomial-denominator forms support this adaptation.
Multiplying both main parts by x gives (3x−2)/(2x+5). Original denominators exclude x=0 and x=−5/2. This adapts C3 Foundation Q2g.
Clearing x² gives (x²−6x)/(x²−36)=x(x−6)/[(x−6)(x+6)]=x/(x+6). Original restrictions remain x≠0,±6. This follows the worked LCD and factorisation method.
Clearing x(x+5) gives [(x+5)+x]/[(x+5)−x]=(2x+5)/5. The original main denominator is 5/[x(x+5)], so x≠0,−5 suffices. This adapts C3 Development Q10b.
Rewriting reciprocal powers and clearing p²q² gives (pq²−p²q)/(q²−p²)=pq(q−p)/[(q−p)(q+p)]=pq/(p+q). Original restrictions are p,q≠0 and p≠±q. C3 Mastery Q11 supports this method.
With x≠0,2, the equation becomes (x+3)/(x−2)=2. Thus x+3=2x−4 and x=7. Substitution gives (10/7)/(5/7)=2. This adapts C3 Foundation Q5.

The innermost denominator is (x+1)/x; its quotient is 2x/(x+1). The outer denominator becomes (3x+1)/(x+1), giving (x+1)/(3x+1). Original restrictions are x≠0,−1,−1/3. Successive simplification follows C3's alternative method and Mastery Q12.
The average is [(1/n)+(1/(n+4))]/2=(2n+4)/[2n(n+4)]=(n+2)/[n(n+4)], with n≠0,−4. This adapts C3 Foundation Q6.
